persona: Buyer for an online t-shirt shop

designs.title: Barley and Malt
designs.why: Clean engraved botanical plate that reads well as a thumbnail and on the tee. It is a gift-friendly item for homebrewers and craft-beer fans, and it works on white and black. At 3 m it is a tidy, airy grid, but there is no hook in one word.
designs.fix: Add a small header line (e.g. BARLEY & MALT or MALTING) so the listing image and the back say beer at a glance.

designs.title: Vitis vinifera
designs.why: The vine and grapes are attractive and wine is a big gift market. The generic WINE bottle and glass make it read like clip art, and the full-size crop shows fine halftone dots across the grapes and bottle. Those dots will clog or drop out in one-ink print, so the $50 tee will look muddier than the mockup.
designs.fix: Redraw the shading as line engraving instead of halftone dots, and swap the generic WINE bottle for a cleaner vine-only plate or a period wine press.

designs.title: Fermentation
designs.why: Nerdy homebrewer appeal and the line work is crisp. But it reads as a textbook page: the chart, the phase table and many small labels shrink to noise on the back. The modern conical steel tank is not romantic enough for a $50 tee.
designs.fix: Cut the graph and phase table and enlarge the fermenter cutaway with a few big labels, so one strong image carries the back.

designs.title: Oak Barrel
designs.why: A barrel is an instantly readable icon for whiskey and wine buyers, and the blueprint style is sharp and prints cleanly. On black it looks like a proper workshop drawing. The many small hoop drawings and text blocks make the lower half busy and thin from a distance.
designs.fix: Shrink or drop the three hoop detail rows and make the elevation and exploded staves larger, so the barrel dominates the print.

designs.title: Pot Still
designs.why: The strongest seller here. It has a bold, heavy-line copper still, fire and worm tub that read from 3 m and look great on white. Whiskey fans are a high-spend gift audience, and the labels are big enough to read. Since it holds up on black, it is a shame not to offer it there.
designs.fix: Offer it on the black tee as well; the dense line work carries in a light ink and doubles the listing.

designs.title: Joiner's Tools
designs.why: A vintage tool catalogue is a proven evergreen seller for dads and woodworkers. The engraving is crisp and the No./size captions add charm. On the back it is a bit small and scattered, with white space around the brace and saw. Some captions, like MALLET and PANEL SAW, sit close together.
designs.fix: Tighten the layout into a fuller block (larger tools, even spacing) and add a small catalogue header such as JOINER'S TOOLS to anchor it.

designs.title: Shaping
designs.why: It is the most lifestyle and emotional piece, and surf sells. But the figure is rendered in photo-style halftone dither, and the crop shows the hands, foam dust and legs dissolving into fine dots. That will print soft and blotchy in one ink. The respirator face is also off-putting as the hero of a shirt.
designs.fix: Rework it as true line engraving with solid blacks and clear hatching instead of dither, and drop the respirator so the shaper reads as a person.

designs.title: Motorcycle
designs.why: Café-racer and classic-bike buyers spend well, and the side view is iconic and clean on black. The sheet is crowded with five detail views plus a spec table and parts list. Those shrink to tiny type on the back, and the carb and sprocket line work is a bit lumpy at full size.
designs.fix: Enlarge the bike to dominate the sheet and keep at most two detail views, dropping the spec table and parts list.
